title: Behaviour Change Journey
description: Applied Kahneman and Fogg's behaviour change frameworks with Harvard Medical School to redesign a health service user journey around moments of high motivation and low-friction actions, rather than usability improvements alone.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: Telefonica Alpha, in collaboration with Harvard Medical School. Applying behaviour change science to health product journey design.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Health products were being built and measured on the wrong thing. Teams were optimising for usability and engagement metrics while clinical outcomes barely moved. The product problem was strategic: investment was going into screen-level improvements that had no meaningful impact on whether patients actually changed behaviour. For Telefonica Alpha and later Koa Health, this mattered commercially — NHS and pharma partners cared about health outcomes, not app ratings.

sections.title: My role
sections.body: I owned the product strategy for how behaviour change would be embedded into the service. I ran workshops with Harvard Medical School to identify which frameworks applied to our patient populations, then translated those into product requirements and specific touchpoint decisions. This was a product direction call, not a design task — it determined what the service did and when, not how it looked.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: The framework drew on Kahneman's research on cognitive biases and BJ Fogg's Behaviour Model (behaviour = motivation + ability + prompt). The product decision was to identify moments of high motivation in the patient journey — after a health scare, at the start of a new treatment, following a positive result — and build the service to act at those moments with low-friction prompts. I defined specific intervention types for each stage: commitment devices at enrolment, progress indicators during use, social norms at drop-off risk points, and individually timed reminders rather than fixed schedules. These became product requirements, not design recommendations.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: The journey design framework was adopted as a standard approach for health product design at Telefonica Alpha and subsequently at Koa Health. It directly influenced the design of the Perspectives programme structure and the engagement approach in Fluid, where the time-mood connection was designed as a behaviour change tool rather than a tracking feature.
